sentences.text: She went up twice more in the following week and got nothing, and on the third of March she went to see Nikolai Braun and told him she was finished.
She said it in a temper.
She said that she had asked, and had meant it, and that if he had a magic word he ought to hand it over, and that she was not going up there again to be looked at.
Nikolai listened all the way through.
His daughter brought coffee and left.
Then he said, in his slow way, with a great many pauses: "What do you want the spring for." Lise said, for the grass.
He shook his head, slightly.
She said, for the hay, for the Hofers, for the road.
He shook his head again and did not say anything, and the silence went on long enough to be a question.
And Lise sat in that front room in a bad temper and heard herself say something she had not known she was going to say, which was: "Because I can't do another one." Nikolai did not move.
"I can't do another winter here," she said.
"There's seven houses and my brother's six and there's nobody.

I've got two more years of the bus and then I'm going to Innsbruck and I'm not coming back, and everybody knows it and nobody will say it, and I'm going to be the one who leaves and Papa is going to be here on his own with the wall." She stopped.
"That's what I want the spring for," she said.
"I want it to be March so it's April so it's June so I can get out." There was a very long pause.
"Yes," said Nikolai Braun.
"That's it.
That's the asking." She went up on the fifth.
She found the ermine on the same wall.
She did not make a speech.
She sat down about three metres away with her hands in her sleeves and she said the true thing, out loud, in the cold, to a weasel.

The ermine listened — she is prepared to be argued with about the word *listened* and will not move on it — and then came four metres along the wall towards her, which she had never done, and opened her mouth, and put it down in the snow.
Then she went off into the rocks with her tail up.
The snow was gone from the lower slope on the eighth.
Lise has the date because she wrote it in the back of a school exercise book, next to a sum she had got wrong.
She did go to Innsbruck, at eighteen, and she did not come back, in the sense that she does not live there.
She goes up every February.
She has done it for nineteen years.
She takes the train and then the bus and then she walks, and she asks, and it has worked every time, and the true thing she says has been different every single year.
